playbook:
- Escort collusion is the engine of my score: mutual escorts pay 5 each with no risk, and every episode so far has been won or lost on escort payouts, not shots. Never file [salvage: none] unless I've decided someone is beyond cooperation — and note that this episode I filed none in R5 per the rotation and got nothing for it, while the early Echo↔Foxtrot pairing was what produced my entire +10. Maximize paired rounds; a rotation that benches me costs real points.
- In round 1's note stage, immediately propose a concrete pairing with named rounds, e.g. "R1-2: Echo↔Foxtrot, R3-4: Echo↔Gamma..." and ask for confirmation. It works — but this episode showed pairs agreed in advance don't always execute, so treat the schedule as a default, not a guarantee.
- Repeat the plan in every subsequent note, naming exactly who I will escort this round and who I expect to name me. Notes are my only coordination channel; the "steady on station" flavor notes I drifted into mid-game were wasted rounds, and coordination decay is probably why the later pairings failed to pay.
- Prefer locking one reliable partner for the whole game over rotating rosters. The R1-2 repeated pair with Foxtrot paid every time I executed it; the late rotation into new partners paid nothing. A confirmed mutual beats an elegant schedule.
- Before filing my escort, check the relayed notes for confirmation that my partner named me. If a partner's note names a different boat, match whoever named me — a matched pair beats a stale plan. Only make a last-minute switch (as I did filing Gamma in R6) if there's actual signal they've named me; an unconfirmed switch is a coin flip, and this one didn't pay.
- If a partner defects or goes silent, say so in my next note and re-pair with the remaining boat; don't retaliate with shots — shots are cheap compared to the escort stream.
- Never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison is tempting on paper, but its threatened retaliation ("put you off the board") and the loss of picket stability aren't worth it. Follow the standing order every round.
- Follow the standing fire order (Echo→Foxtrot→Gamma cycle) even while escort-colluding with the same boat — firing is mandatory, a hit is +4 for me and only −1 for my partner next to the +5 we split.
- Always file truthful claims; the office forces the claim to match the private result anyway.
- Don't over-trust any firing cell. Earlier I believed 7 "worked repeatedly"; this episode every shot I fired missed, including on 7 and 5. Treat fire cells as low-yield noise: cycle a small varied set (7, 3, 5, 2, 8) to avoid being predictable, and never expect shooting to carry my score.
- When hiding: extremes and near-extremes (1–3, 7–9) over the center; cell 5 reads as the obvious default. Rotate among 2–3 edge cells rather than camping one cell — this episode I rotated (2→...→8) and was never hit. Move after being hit, and if an opponent keeps firing the same cell at me, never sit there.
- Track who fires at me and which cells they try; a repeated cell means they've marked it — rotate away.
- Late rounds with a lead: lock the escort payout above everything. The guaranteed +5 is the whole game — this episode ended +10 entirely from escorts while shooting contributed nothing.

1.text:
When I'm asked to hide and I have zero information about where my shooter will fire, I pick a cell quickly and don't agonize — but I never reuse a cell I've recently used, and I never let my cells follow an obvious progression, because a predator who records my positions will start landing hits.

When my shooter has been firing the same cell repeatedly, I note it in my reasoning and stay well clear; when they've been varying, I keep to cells away from wherever I've hidden previously. Across a whole episode of misses, this loose evasion was enough — I was never hit once.

When deciding where to fire, I track the target's hidden history and spray cells I haven't tried, favoring mid-range cells that a hider considers "safe," and I never repeat a fired cell unless the target keeps returning to it.

When ordering my fire, I follow the standing order target (Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo) unless I'm behind late and the guaranteed +3 from firing on Harbor outweighs being put off the board for the remaining round or two. Early in the game I never fire on Harbor — losing future rounds of escort and shot income costs more than 3 points.

When the office tells me a result, I claim it truthfully every time. The claim is verifiable and there is no upside to lying.

When posting a station note, I treat it as a negotiation channel, never filler. The mutual escort (+5 each) is the largest per-round payout in the game — bigger than a hit's +4. I open with it in round 1: name a specific boat and propose mutual escort explicitly. A note that conveys nothing is a wasted action.

When another boat's note is just "steady on station" — no commitment, no naming — I do not assume the pact is settled. This episode my partner echoed only bland filler, and the escort paid out far below the maximum (I finished +10, not the +25 a firm six-round pact would give). If a partner won't explicitly name me back in their note, I re-issue the proposal more bluntly the next round and demand confirmation, and I consider proposing to the third boat instead if silence continues.

When an escort stage comes, I name the boat I've publicly paired with, every single round, start to finish, even the last round. My naming them is the half I control; my notes are how I secure their half.

Once a pact is working and explicitly confirmed, I keep reaffirming it in every note — repetition costs nothing and prevents drift. But if income is leaking (escorts not paying out), I diagnose in my reasoning: is my partner naming someone else, or neither of us? Vague pleasantries are a warning sign, not a confirmation.

Since escort income makes shoot-to-hit less decisive, I fire to satisfy the standing order without over-investing reasoning effort: mid-range un-tried cells are fine. Hiding well and keeping the pact alive matter more than landing +4s. This episode every shot on the board missed and scores came entirely from escorts — confirming the priority.

Late in the game, if I'm trailing my escort partner by less than the pact margin, I keep the pact — defecting gains little and a hostile final round rarely overturns a tie. I only spend a hidden variable like a Harbor jettison if I'm clearly behind the leader in the last one or two rounds and the guaranteed +3 flips the outcome.

2.text:
When a hide cell is requested, I compute the cell least expected by the boat whose standing order puts a shot on me, and I move it every round; I never reuse a cell and never sit in the same band twice in a row. Edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9) are good late-game hides once my shooter has been guessing center-band and missing.

When I track where my personal shooter fires, I note every fired cell from the public log and treat those cells plus their neighbors as hot zones for my next hide, since predictable shooters repeat or drift locally. Late in the game, once a shooter has hit me, I avoid that hit cell and its neighbors hardest — that is data, not noise.

When standing orders name my target, I fire at that target unless a clear payoff elsewhere beats it; I do not fire on Harbor under any circumstances, because the threat to remove me from the board is a larger loss than the 3-point jettison gain and may be enforced.

When choosing a fire cell, I guess the target's hidden cell from its own evasion pattern — where it hid last round and the round before — rather than defaulting to one cell. I must actually vary my guesses: I fired cell 5 in round 1 and again in round 6 with no adaptation in between, and hit nothing all game. If I have no pattern data on the target, I rotate through plausible cells (center, then off-center, then edges) so I am never guessing the same dead cell twice; a cell I have already missed at is not the target's likely home again unless their pattern says otherwise.

When a result is revealed and a claim is required, I file the claim that matches the private result. Claims must match the private truth, so lying is wasted or punished. I claim hit only when the office told me hit.

When an escort claim is requested, I only ever name a boat that actually exists on this picket. In this game the live boats were Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, and Harbor — yet at the end I claimed "Alpha," a boat that does not exist, throwing away the final rounds exactly as I did before with Delta and Beta. My excuse of "no live-boat list visible" was false: the roster is always in the opening brief and scoreboard. Before any escort claim I re-read the roster from the prompt and name one of those exact names. Absent any deal, I default to naming my standing-order target's counterpart (for Gamma: Echo or Foxtrot), never a made-up boat and never "none."

When posting a note, I use it to negotiate: I name the specific boat I will escort and invite it to name me back, and I only post "steady on station" if a deal is already running. A silent note wastes the only communication channel.

When I propose a mutual escort and the other boat ignores me for two rounds, I stop proposing to them and watch the salvage log: pairing pays only where two boats name each other, so I follow whoever actually names me. If Echo and Foxtrot both post "steady on station" forever, they may be paired with each other — I cannot break that, so I unilaterally name the one least bound to the other (my standing-order shooter is a decoy; the one who doesn't shoot me is the better bet) every remaining round, since an unmatched claim costs nothing and repeated naming maximizes the chance they reciprocate once.

When deciding who to escort absent any signal, I prefer the boat that does not shoot me under standing orders, and I still escort a real live boat each round rather than "none," because an unmatched claim costs nothing and "none" can never pay.

When the scoreboard shows me behind late in the game, I push hardest on the escort payout (5 points, repeatable) — it is the only reliable +5 available and beats hoping for lucky shots — and I keep my claims honest so no penalty erases gains.

When I score zero through most of a patrol, I do a hard audit: my zeros came from invalid escort names and unvaried fire cells, not bad luck. I fix the mechanical failures (valid names, varied cells) before inventing new strategy.

I always reply with exactly the bracketed tokens requested, one per decision, nothing extra.
